questions.question: Coordination number of a particle in body centred cubic packing is
questions.answer:
**(C)** 8

In a body-centred cubic lattice the atom at the body centre touches the eight atoms at the corners of the cube, so its coordination number is 8. (For comparison: simple cubic 6, f.c.c./h.c.p. 12.) The b.c.c. unit cell contains $8\times\frac18+1=2$ atoms and has a packing efficiency of 68%.

questions.question: The value of order of a reaction can be
questions.answer:
**(D)** all of these

Order is defined by experiment, not by the balanced equation, so it may be positive, zero or fractional — e.g. 1 for a first-order reaction, 0 for the decomposition of NH$_3$ on platinum, $\frac32$ for $\ce{CO + Cl2 -> COCl2}$. It may even be negative when a species inhibits the reaction. Negative or fractional orders are possible because order is the sum of the exponents in the experimentally determined rate law.

questions.question: For a chemical reaction $\ce{A -> B}$ it is found that the rate of reaction does not change when the concentration of A is doubled. The order of reaction with respect to A is
questions.answer:
**(C)** zero

If rate $=k[A]^n$ and doubling $[A]$ leaves the rate unchanged, then $2^n=1$, so $n=0$. The rate is independent of the concentration of A, i.e. the reaction is zero order in A — typical of surface-catalysed or photochemical reactions where the rate is set by the catalyst surface or by light intensity, not by the reactant concentration.

questions.question: Which of the following is a lyophobic colloid?
questions.answer:
**(B)** Sulphur

A sulphur sol is **lyophobic** — the dispersed sulphur particles have no affinity for the dispersion medium, the sol cannot be made by simple mixing, and it is coagulated readily by electrolytes. Gelatin, starch and gum arabic are all lyophilic (they are large molecules that hydrate strongly and form reversible, stable sols).

questions.question: Which of the following ores is concentrated by froth floatation process?
questions.answer:
**(C)** Copper pyrite

Froth floatation separates **sulphide ores** from earthy gangue: the powdered ore is stirred with water, pine oil and a collector, and air is blown through. Sulphide particles become preferentially wetted by the oil, cling to the air bubbles and rise as a froth, while the siliceous gangue settles. Copper pyrite (CuFeS$_2$) is the classic case; hematite, magnetite and bauxite are oxide ores, concentrated by magnetic separation or leaching.

questions.question: Which of the following is the least stable hydride?
questions.answer:
**(D)** SbH$_3$

Down group 15 the M–H bond becomes longer and weaker as the atomic size increases (N > P > As > Sb), so the thermal stability of the hydrides falls in the order $\ce{NH3 > PH3 > AsH3 > SbH3}$. Stibine, $\ce{SbH3}$, is therefore the least stable — it decomposes even at room temperature — and the hydrides become correspondingly better reducing agents down the group.

questions.question: Oxidation number of Cr in CrO$_4^{2-}$ is
questions.answer:
**(C)** 6

Let the oxidation number of Cr be $x$, with oxygen at −2:

$$x+4(-2)=-2\ \Rightarrow\ x=+6$$

So chromium is in the +6 state in chromate, and equally in dichromate $\ce{Cr2O7^{2-}}$: $2x+7(-2)=-2\Rightarrow x=+6$.

questions.question: Which of the following is an ambidentate ligand?
questions.answer:
**(C)** NO$_2^-$

An **ambidentate** ligand has two possible donor atoms but can use only one at a time. The nitrite ion can bind through nitrogen (nitro, $\ce{-NO2}$) or through oxygen (nitrito, $\ce{-ONO}$), giving linkage isomers. Water (through O), ammonia (through N) and bromide (through Br) each have only one donor site, so they cannot be ambidentate. Thiocyanate, $\ce{SCN^-}$, is another ambidentate ligand.

questions.question: Write down the structural formula of a primary alkyl halide.
questions.answer:
A primary ($1^\circ$) alkyl halide has the halogen attached to a carbon which carries only **one** other carbon — i.e. a $\ce{-CH2X}$ group. Taking ethyl chloride as the simplest example after the methyl halides:

$$\ce{CH3-CH2-Cl}$$

The printed alternative is the same structure written fully:

$$\begin{array}{c}\ce{H\quad H}\\ \ce{|\quad|}\\ \ce{H-C-C-Cl}\\ \ce{|\quad|}\\ \ce{H\quad H}\end{array}$$

Such a compound gives an S$_N$2 reaction readily (the primary carbon is unhindered) and does not readily eliminate.

questions.question: Secondary alcohol on oxidation gives which compound?
questions.answer:
**A ketone.**

A secondary alcohol has the $\ce{-CH(OH)-}$ group on a carbon carrying two other carbon atoms; oxidation removes the two hydrogens from that carbon and gives a carbonyl carbon bearing two alkyl groups:

$$\ce{R2CHOH ->[O] R2C=O}$$

For example, propan-2-ol gives propanone. Ketones resist further oxidation under mild conditions (a C–C bond would have to be broken), whereas primary alcohols give aldehydes and then carboxylic acids, and tertiary alcohols are not oxidised at the carbinol carbon at all.

questions.question: Write down the I.U.P.A.C. name of PhCH$_2$CH$_2$COOH.
questions.answer:
**3-Phenylpropanoic acid.**

The parent chain is the three-carbon acid, $\ce{CH2-CH2-COOH}$ numbered from the carboxyl carbon as C-1; the phenyl substituent sits on C-3:

$$\ce{Ph-CH2-CH2-COOH}\quad\text{=}\quad\text{3-phenylpropanoic acid}$$

(The trivial name is hydrocinnamic acid.)

questions.question: What is the hybridization of N in R$_3$N?
questions.answer:
**sp$^3$.**

In a tertiary amine the nitrogen has three $\sigma$ bonds to the alkyl groups and a lone pair; three bonded atoms plus one lone pair make a steric number of 4, so the nitrogen is $sp^3$ hybridised and the geometry about it is pyramidal (bond angles close to 109.5°). The lone pair is available for donation, which is why amines are basic and nucleophilic.

questions.question: Write down the name of the product obtained on hydrolysis of lactose.
questions.answer:
**D-Galactose and D-glucose** (in equimolar amounts).

Lactose is a disaccharide of galactose and glucose joined by a $\beta$-1,4-glycosidic bond; boiling it with dilute acid, or treatment with the enzyme lactase, hydrolyses this bond:

$$\ce{C12H22O11 + H2O -> C6H12O6(galactose) + C6H12O6(glucose)}$$

Both products are reducing sugars.

questions.question: Name the monomer of Nylon-66.
questions.answer:
**Hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid** (1,6-diaminohexane, $\ce{H2N-(CH2)6-NH2}$, and hexane-1,6-dioic acid, $\ce{HOOC-(CH2)4-COOH}$).

These two bifunctional monomers condense with the loss of water in a 1:1 mole ratio to give the polyamide Nylon-6,6 — the '6,6' referring to the six carbons in each monomer:

$$\ce{nH2N(CH2)6NH2 + nHOOC(CH2)4COOH -> [-NH(CH2)6NH-CO(CH2)4CO-]_n + 2nH2O}$$

Nylon-6,6 is a tough, strong fibre with a high melting point because of intermolecular hydrogen bonding between the amide groups.

questions.question: Name a hypnotic drug.
questions.answer:
**Veronal (barbital)** — the first of the barbiturate hypnotics and sedatives; others are **Luminal (phenobarbital)**, **Seconal** and **Valium (diazepam)**.

Barbiturates are derivatives of barbituric acid and act as central nervous system depressants; they induce sleep at low doses and are used as sedatives, though they carry a risk of dependence. Valium belongs to the benzodiazepine class and is used as a tranquilliser.

questions.question: How does molar conductivity change with concentration in the case of (i) weak electrolyte (ii) strong electrolyte?
questions.answer:
**(i) Weak electrolyte.** The molar conductivity increases **steeply** with dilution and without limit as the concentration approaches zero, because the degree of ionisation $\alpha$ rises sharply with dilution — at infinite dilution the electrolyte is effectively completely ionised and $\Lambda_m$ reaches $\Lambda_m^\infty$.

**(ii) Strong electrolyte.** The electrolyte is already fully ionised, so ionic mobility alone changes: $\Lambda_m$ increases only **slowly and linearly** with $\sqrt{c}$ (Debye–Hückel–Onsager behaviour) as interionic attractions are removed on dilution.

$$\Lambda_m=\Lambda_m^\infty-A\sqrt{c}$$

Hence the plot of $\Lambda_m$ against $\sqrt c$ is a straight line for a strong electrolyte, while for a weak electrolyte it is strongly curved and $\Lambda_m^\infty$ cannot be obtained by simple extrapolation (Kohlrausch's law of independent ion migration is used instead).

questions.question: What is the difference between roasting and calcination?
questions.answer:
| Roasting | Calcination |
|---|---|
| The ore is heated **strongly in the presence of excess air** | The ore is heated **in the absence or limited supply of air** |
| Applied to **sulphide ores** | Applied to **carbonate and hydrated oxide ores** |
| Sulphide is converted to the oxide, SO$_2$ being evolved: $\ce{2ZnS + 3O2 -> 2ZnO + 2SO2}$ | Carbonate or hydroxide decomposes to the oxide, CO$_2$/H$_2$O being lost: $\ce{ZnCO3 -> ZnO + CO2}$ |
| An oxidation process | A thermal decomposition (not an oxidation) |
| Temperature required is generally higher | Carried out just below the melting point of the ore |

Both are preliminary steps for converting an ore into the oxide from which the metal is then reduced.

questions.question: Give balanced equation of the following: (i) $\ce{I2 + NaIO3}$ (ii) $\ce{I2 + Na2S2O3}$
questions.answer:
**(i) Iodine with sodium iodate.** Iodate is already the highest oxide of iodine in this medium, and iodine is not oxidised further by it — the two do not react appreciably in neutral solution:

$$\ce{I2 + NaIO3 -> \text{no reaction}}$$

What does happen readily is the **reverse** comproportionation in acid: iodate oxidises iodide to free iodine, which is why acidified iodate liberates iodine from KI:

$$\ce{IO3^- + 5I^- + 6H^+ -> 3I2 + 3H2O}$$

If a strong oxidising agent such as chlorate is used instead, iodine is carried up to iodate, as the printed key has it:

$$\ce{I2 + 2NaClO3 -> 2NaIO3 + Cl2}$$

**(ii) Iodine with sodium thiosulphate** — this is the classic iodometric titration. Thiosulphate is oxidised to tetrathionate while iodine is reduced to iodide:

$$\ce{I2 + 2Na2S2O3 -> 2NaI + Na2S4O6}$$

The deep brown colour of iodine is discharged, and the reaction is quantitative, so it is used to estimate iodine and hence the strength of any oxidising agent that liberates iodine from KI.

questions.question: What happens when aqueous ammonia reacts with (i) Mercury (I) chloride (ii) Mercury (II) chloride?
questions.answer:
(i) **Mercury(I) chloride (calomel), $\ce{Hg2Cl2}$**, with aqueous ammonia gives a **black** precipitate — a mixture of finely divided mercury and white mercury(II) amido chloride:

$$\ce{Hg2Cl2 + 2NH3 -> Hg(NH2)Cl + Hg + NH4Cl}$$

The overall appearance is black (the finely divided mercury) mixed with white, and this is the basis of the test that distinguishes it from the mercury(II) salt.

(ii) **Mercury(II) chloride (corrosive sublimate), $\ce{HgCl2}$**, with aqueous ammonia gives a **white** precipitate of mercury(II) amido chloride:

$$\ce{HgCl2 + 2NH3 -> Hg(NH2)Cl v + NH4Cl}$$

The difference in colour (black versus white) is a standard test to distinguish the two chlorides of mercury.

questions.question: What are transition elements? Why do transition elements show variation in oxidation number?
questions.answer:
**Transition elements** are the d-block elements whose atoms or ions have an **incompletely filled d subshell** in the ground state or in one of their common oxidation states. Their general electronic configuration is $(n-1)d^{1-9}ns^{1-2}$; Sc, Ti and Cu are examples. Because the d orbitals are available and the energies of the 4s and 3d orbitals are close, electrons from both shells can take part in bonding.

**Why the oxidation number varies:** the $(n-1)d$ electrons and the $ns$ electrons have comparable energies, so a variable number of them can be lost or shared without a great energy penalty. Successive electrons can thus be removed, giving a series of oxidation states differing by one — Fe$^{2+}$/Fe$^{3+}$, Mn$^{2+}$ to Mn$^{7+}$, Cr$^{3+}$/Cr$^{6+}$. The stability of a particular state depends on the balance between the ionisation enthalpies (which rise) and the hydration and lattice enthalpies (which also rise), together with the extra stability of half-filled ($d^5$) and completely filled ($d^{10}$) configurations.

questions.question: Define the following: (i) Linkage Isomerism (ii) Hydrate Isomerism.
questions.answer:
(i) **Linkage (ionisation) isomerism** arises in complexes containing an **ambidentate ligand**, which can attach to the metal through either of two donor atoms. The two isomers have the same molecular formula but differ in which atom is bonded, giving different properties:

$$\ce{[Co(NH3)5(NO2)]Cl2}\quad\text{(nitro, N-bonded)}$$

$$\ce{[Co(NH3)5(ONO)]Cl2}\quad\text{(nitrito, O-bonded)}$$

The nitrite ligand may be bonded through N or through O; similarly thiocyanate may be S- or N-bonded.

(ii) **Hydrate (solvate) isomerism** occurs when water molecules can be inside or outside the coordination sphere; the isomers have the same formula but differ in the number of water molecules coordinated to the metal, and hence in colour and in the conductivity of their solutions:

$$\ce{[Co(H2O)6]Cl3}\quad\text{(violet)}$$

$$\ce{[Co(H2O)5Cl]Cl2.H2O}\quad\text{(green) — one Cl entered the sphere}$$

$$\ce{[Co(H2O)4Cl2]Cl.2H2O}$$

Each successive replacement of a coordinated H$_2$O by Cl inside the sphere lowers the number of free ions, so the molar conductivity of the three falls in the same order.

questions.question: What are synthetic polymers? Name any two synthetic polymers. / What is natural rubber? Write down the name and structural formula of its monomer.
questions.answer:
**Synthetic polymers** are man-made macromolecules built by joining many small monomer units through polymerisation (addition or condensation). Unlike natural polymers they can be tailored for particular properties, and examples include **Nylon-6, Nylon-6,6, Buna-S, PVC and Bakelite**.

**Natural rubber** is a linear polymer of **isoprene (2-methylbuta-1,3-diene)**, obtained as latex from the bark of the rubber tree (*Hevea brasiliensis*). Its repeating unit is cis-1,4-polyisoprene:

$$\ce{CH2=C(CH3)-CH=CH2}\qquad\text{(isoprene monomer)}$$

$$\ce{[-CH2-C(CH3)=CH-CH2-]_n}\qquad\text{(natural rubber)}$$

Vulcanisation — heating with sulphur — introduces sulphur bridges between the chains, making the rubber harder, stronger and less sticky.

questions.question: What is a disinfectant? Name any two disinfectants.
questions.answer:
**Disinfectants** are chemicals which kill or prevent the growth of micro-organisms and are applied to **inanimate objects** such as floors, drains, instruments and toilets (not to living tissue — that is the role of antiseptics).

Examples: **phenol (carbolic acid)** and **chlorine** (as bleaching powder or a hypochlorite solution); others are Dettol (chloroxylenol), formaldehyde and sulphur dioxide. Phenol was the first surgical disinfectant (Lister) and is the standard against which others are compared, using the phenol coefficient.

questions.question: Define the following: (i) Conductor (ii) Insulator (iii) Semiconductor.
questions.answer:
(i) **Conductor.** A substance that allows electric current to pass through it to a large extent — its electrical conductivity is high (of the order of $10^{4}$–$10^{6}\ \Omega^{-1}$cm$^{-1}$) because the valence band overlaps the conduction band so charge carriers are plentiful. Metals such as copper, silver and aluminium are conductors.

(ii) **Insulator.** A solid in which the conduction band is separated from the valence band by a wide forbidden gap (about 5–6 eV), so practically no electrons can cross it; the conductivity is negligible ($\sim10^{-12}\ \Omega^{-1}$cm$^{-1}$ or less). Diamond, glass and rubber are insulators.

(iii) **Semiconductor.** A solid whose conductivity lies between that of a conductor and an insulator (of the order of $10^{-5}$–$10^{2}\ \Omega^{-1}$cm$^{-1}$), because the forbidden gap is small (~1 eV) and electrons can be promoted thermally. Silicon and germanium are the examples, and their conductivity increases with temperature and with doping.

questions.question: What is corrosion? What are the factors which affect corrosion?
questions.answer:
**Corrosion** is the slow, spontaneous destruction of a metal by the chemical action of the surrounding environment — the metal is converted into compounds such as oxides, sulphides, carbonates or sulphates. Rusting of iron (hydrated ferric oxide, $\ce{Fe2O3.xH2O}$) is the commonest example:

$$\ce{4Fe + 3O2 + xH2O -> 2Fe2O3.xH2O}$$

**Factors that promote corrosion**

1. **Reactivity of the metal** — the more electropositive the metal, the more readily it is oxidised.
2. **Presence of impurities** — impurities set up tiny galvanic cells, so impure iron rusts faster than pure iron.
3. **Presence of air (oxygen) and moisture** — both are essential for rusting; dry air or perfectly dry oxygen causes no rust.
4. **Presence of an electrolyte** — dissolved salts and acids raise the conductivity of the moisture film and accelerate the electrochemical process; this is why iron rusts faster in seawater.
5. **Strain and surface condition** — stressed regions become anodic, and a rough surface exposes more area.

Corrosion can be prevented by painting, greasing, galvanising (a zinc coating), electroplating, or by cathodic protection.

questions.question: The values of $\Lambda^\infty_m$ of NH$_4$Cl, NaOH and NaCl at infinite dilution are 129.8, 248.1 and 126.4 S cm$^2$ mol$^{-1}$. Find the value of $\Lambda^\infty_m$ for NH$_4$OH.
questions.answer:
By **Kohlrausch's law**, at infinite dilution each ion migrates independently, so the molar conductivity of an electrolyte is the sum of the ionic conductivities:

$$\Lambda_m^\infty(\ce{NH4Cl})=\lambda^\infty_{\ce{NH4+}}+\lambda^\infty_{\ce{Cl-}}=129.8$$

$$\Lambda_m^\infty(\ce{NaOH})=\lambda^\infty_{\ce{Na+}}+\lambda^\infty_{\ce{OH-}}=248.1$$

$$\Lambda_m^\infty(\ce{NaCl})=\lambda^\infty_{\ce{Na+}}+\lambda^\infty_{\ce{Cl-}}=126.4$$

Adding the first two and subtracting the third cancels both Na$^+$ and Cl$^-$:

$$\Lambda_m^\infty(\ce{NH4OH})=\Lambda_m^\infty(\ce{NH4Cl})+\Lambda_m^\infty(\ce{NaOH})-\Lambda_m^\infty(\ce{NaCl})$$

$$=129.8+248.1-126.4=251.5\ \text{S cm}^{2}\text{mol}^{-1}$$

**So $\Lambda_m^\infty$ for NH$_4$OH is 251.5 S cm$^2$ mol$^{-1}$** — a value that cannot be measured directly, because NH$_4$OH is a weak electrolyte whose $\Lambda_m$ curve never reaches a limiting value by extrapolation.

questions.question: Explain the difference between physisorption and chemisorption.
questions.answer:
| Physisorption | Chemisorption |
|---|---|
| Caused by weak van der Waals forces | Caused by forces of the strength of a chemical bond |
| Occurs at low temperature and is exothermic with a low heat of adsorption (20–40 kJ/mol) | Occurs at high temperature, with a high heat of adsorption (80–240 kJ/mol) |
| Needs little or no activation energy; fast and reversible | Needs a significant activation energy; slow and largely irreversible |
| Multilayer adsorption is possible | Only a monolayer can form |
| Not specific — any gas on any surface | Highly specific, as in a chemical reaction |

For example, hydrogen on charcoal is physisorbed (it can be pumped off easily), while hydrogen on nickel is chemisorbed as Ni–H bonds.

questions.question: Complete the following: (i) $\ce{CH3-CH2-CH2-Cl + NaI ->[acetone][heat]}$ (ii) $\ce{CH3-CH2-CH2-Br + NaOH ->[water]}$ (iii) $\ce{CH3-CH2-Br + KCN ->[H2O/ethanol]}$
questions.answer:
(i) **Finkelstein reaction** — sodium iodide in dry acetone displaces the chloride, since NaI is soluble in acetone while NaCl is not, so the equilibrium is driven forward:

$$\ce{CH3CH2CH2Cl + NaI ->[acetone] CH3CH2CH2I + NaCl v}$$

(ii) **Hydrolysis by aqueous alkali** gives the alcohol (nucleophilic substitution):

$$\ce{CH3CH2CH2Br + NaOH(aq) ->[\Delta] CH3CH2CH2OH + NaBr}$$

(iii) **With potassium cyanide** the cyanide ion displaces bromide and the carbon chain is lengthened by one carbon, giving a nitrile:

$$\ce{CH3CH2Br + KCN ->[H2O/EtOH] CH3CH2CN + KBr}$$

Hydrolysis of the propionitrile so obtained would give propanoic acid.

questions.question: How will you bring about the following conversions? (i) Propene → Propan-2-ol (ii) Benzyl chloride → Benzyl alcohol (iii) Ethyl magnesium bromide → 2-methylpropan-2-ol
questions.answer:
(i) **Propene → propan-2-ol:** acid-catalysed hydration follows Markovnikov's rule, the OH going to the more substituted carbon:

$$\ce{CH3-CH=CH2 + H2O ->[H2SO4] CH3-CH(OH)-CH3}$$

(ii) **Benzyl chloride → benzyl alcohol:** hydrolysis with aqueous alkali (S$_N$1, the benzylic cation being stabilised by the ring):

$$\ce{C6H5CH2Cl + NaOH(aq) -> C6H5CH2OH + NaCl}$$

(iii) **Ethyl magnesium bromide → 2-methylpropan-2-ol:** the Grignard reagent adds to propanone, and the resulting alkoxide is hydrolysed:

$$\ce{CH3MgBr + (CH3)2C=O -> (CH3)3C-OMgBr ->[H3O^+] (CH3)3C-OH}$$

A tertiary alcohol is obtained because the carbonyl carbon of acetone carries two methyl groups already.

questions.question: Complete the following: (i) $\ce{C6H5NH2 + CHCl3 + KOH ->}$ (ii) $\ce{C6H5N2Cl + C2H5OH ->}$ (iii) $\ce{C6H5NH2 + HNO2 ->}$
questions.answer:
(i) **Carbylamine (Hoffmann isocyanide) reaction** — only primary amines respond:

$$\ce{C6H5NH2 + CHCl3 + 3KOH -> C6H5NC + 3KCl + 3H2O}$$

The product is **phenyl isocyanide**, with a foul smell — the basis of the test.

(ii) **Reduction of the diazonium salt by ethanol** — the diazonium group is replaced by hydrogen and ethanol is oxidised to acetaldehyde:

$$\ce{C6H5N2Cl + C2H5OH -> C6H6 + N2 + CH3CHO + HCl}$$

The product is **benzene**.

(iii) **Diazotisation** at 273–278 K:

$$\ce{C6H5NH2 + HNO2 + HCl ->[273-278 K] C6H5N2^+Cl^- + 2H2O}$$

giving **benzene diazonium chloride**; at higher temperature it decomposes to phenol.

questions.question: Differentiate between globular and fibrous proteins.
questions.answer:
| Globular proteins | Fibrous proteins |
|---|---|
| The polypeptide chain is coiled into a compact, roughly spherical shape | The chains run parallel and are held together in long fibres or sheets |
| Held in shape mainly by hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions and ionic bonds within the chain | Held together by hydrogen bonds **and disulphide bridges between** chains |
| Generally **soluble** in water | Generally **insoluble** in water |
| Sensitive to changes of pH and temperature (they denature easily) | More resistant, mechanically strong |
| Examples: **insulin, albumins, haemoglobin, enzymes** | Examples: **keratin** (hair, wool, nails), **myosin** (muscle), **collagen** (tendons) |

Both are built from the same 20 $\alpha$-amino acids joined by peptide bonds; the difference is the way the chain folds — and hence the biological role, globular proteins acting as enzymes, hormones and carriers while fibrous ones give structure and strength.

questions.question: Discuss the following: (i) Osmosis (ii) Osmotic pressure (iii) Semipermeable membrane. / Boiling point of water at 750 mm Hg is 96.63 °C. How much sucrose (C$_{12}$H$_{22}$O$_{11}$) is to be added to 500 g of water so that it boils at 100 °C? ($K_b$ for water = 0.52 K kg mol$^{-1}$)
questions.answer:
(i) **Osmosis** is the spontaneous flow of **solvent** molecules through a semipermeable membrane from the pure solvent (or a dilute solution) into a more concentrated solution. The solvent moves down its own concentration gradient, and the process continues until the two sides are in equilibrium.

(ii) **Osmotic pressure ($\pi$)** is the minimum excess pressure that must be applied to the solution to just prevent osmosis. For dilute solutions it obeys van't Hoff's equation

$$\pi=CRT=\frac{n}{V}RT$$

where $C$ is the molar concentration. Since colligative in nature, $\pi$ is used to determine molar masses, especially of macromolecules such as proteins.

(iii) **Semipermeable membrane** is a membrane which allows only solvent molecules to pass through it while blocking solute particles — animal bladder, cellophane and parchment paper are examples. It is essential for osmosis to occur.

**Numerical.** The required elevation of boiling point is

$$\Delta T_b=100-96.63=3.37\ ^\circ\text{C}$$

Using $\Delta T_b=K_b m$ with $m=\dfrac{x\times1000}{342\times500}$ (molar mass of sucrose = 342 g mol$^{-1}$):

$$3.37=0.52\times\frac{x\times1000}{342\times500}$$

$$\frac{x\times1000}{342\times500}=\frac{3.37}{0.52}=6.4808$$

$$x=\frac{6.4808\times342\times500}{1000}=\frac{6.4808\times171000}{1000}=1108\ \text{g}$$

**About 1108 g of sucrose** must be dissolved in 500 g of water. (Equivalently, the molality needed is $6.48$ mol kg$^{-1}$, i.e. $6.48\times342=2216$ g per kg of water, which is 1108 g in 500 g.)

questions.question: Complete the following: (i) $\ce{NaCl + H2SO4(conc)} ->$ (ii) $\ce{Na2SO3 + HCl} ->$ (iii) $\ce{Cl2 + H2O} ->$ (iv) $\ce{Cl2 + NaOH(conc) ->[heat]}$ (v) $\ce{Na2S2O3 + H2O + Cl2} ->$ / Draw structure of the following: H$_2$SO$_4$, H$_2$S$_2$O$_7$, HClO$_4$, HClO$_3$, HClO$_2$
questions.answer:
**(i)** In the cold, hydrogen chloride is evolved; on heating the acid sulphate reacts further:

$$\ce{NaCl + H2SO4 -> NaHSO4 + HCl ^}\qquad\text{(cold)}$$

$$\ce{NaHSO4 + NaCl ->[\Delta] Na2SO4 + HCl ^}$$

**(ii)** A weaker acid displaces the stronger one:

$$\ce{Na2SO3 + 2HCl -> 2NaCl + SO2 ^ + H2O}$$

**(iii)** Chlorine disproportionates in water — the basis of chlorine water as an oxidising and bleaching agent:

$$\ce{Cl2 + H2O -> HCl + HOCl}$$

**(iv)** With hot concentrated alkali the disproportionation goes all the way to chlorate:

$$\ce{3Cl2 + 6NaOH(conc) ->[heat] NaClO3 + 5NaCl + 3H2O}$$

**(v)** Thiosulphate is oxidised to sulphate and chlorine is reduced:

$$\ce{Na2S2O3 + H2O + Cl2 -> Na2SO4 + 2HCl + S}$$

**Structures.** In each case the central atom is $sp^3$ hybridised with a tetrahedral arrangement of electron pairs:

- **$\ce{H2SO4}$** — S is surrounded tetrahedrally by two $\ce{S=O}$, two $\ce{S-OH}$; O–H ends are acidic.
- **$\ce{H2S2O7}$ (oleum)** — two $\ce{SO4}$ tetrahedra sharing a corner oxygen, $\ce{HO-SO2-O-SO2-OH}$.
- **$\ce{HClO4}$** — Cl tetrahedrally bonded to four oxygens, three of them terminal $\ce{Cl=O}$, the fourth $\ce{Cl-OH}$; perchloric acid is the strongest common acid.
- **$\ce{HClO3}$** — pyramidal Cl with two terminal $\ce{Cl=O}$ and one $\ce{Cl-OH}$.
- **$\ce{HClO2}$** — bent, with one $\ce{C=O}$-like and one $\ce{Cl-OH}$ bond, an $sp^2$ chlorine.

Acid strength rises with the number of terminal oxygens as $\ce{HClO2 < HClO3 < HClO4}$, since the extra oxygens delocalise the charge on the conjugate base.
